utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, I see that it's you again so changing of the guards have been successful again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We like to ring the changes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Perhaps in the meantime, I could inform the parties about a small change we have discussed with the Registry in the admission of documents in evidence. Madam Registrar usually reads shortly what the exhibit is when it's presented and we'll not read the whole description again once a final decision will be taken, and if any of the parties would have any comment on the way the exhibits are described on the list, we'll take note of that and see whether the description is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that will save some time in the reading, especially if we have a long list of exhibits. Good afternoon, Mr. Trbojevic. Not very polite of me to continue speaking when you enter the courtroom. Good afternoon. I'd like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and I'd like to remind you that if you would think that a truthful answer to the questions put to you might be incriminating for yourself, that you could address the court and tell us that so we can make the determination proper. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the session before we concluded last night, I believe we looked at a number of documents including one from early August by Mr. Kovac, and a document from the Ministry of the Interior dated July 17th. I'd like to turn now to a government session held on the 22nd of July found at tab 34 in binder 1. Mr. Trbojevic, tab 34 contains the minutes of the 41st session of the government held, as I indicated a moment ago, on the 22nd of July, 1992. The minutes indicate that the chairman of the session was Professor Djeric, the Prime Minister, and that among those present were yourself, the government Deputy Prime Minister and Mr. Subotic, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Stanisic, and Dr. Kalinic. If I could ask you, sir, to turn to agenda item 14. That agenda item details current issues and the third issue reflected in the minutes is the following: "The government has been informed on some occurrences of unlawful treatment of war prisoners. It has been concluded that all measures be taken to ensure the consistent application of an order by the Serb Republic of BH Presidency regarding the treatment of prisoners." Mr. Trbojevic, can you tell us what information the government had received regarding occurrences of unlawful treatment of war prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who briefed the government and what information was provided exactly. Based on the agenda items prior to this one, I can see that they are mentioning military police and some other issues and as for this part here, there is nothing more specific than what you quoted. It just says "certain instances of unlawful treatment." I can't remember who specifically said what at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection about the general subject matter being raised around this time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here or rather the decision of the Presidency on treatment to be -- treatment of the war prisoners, that decision is mentioned here so that must mean that some kind of a discussion took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of our earlier discussions about the government sessions, the establishment of the working group to address the question of prisoners and exchanges, do you have a recollection about the receipt of subsequent information regarding unlawful treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Minutes of the session state that all measure should be taken to ensure the application of an order by the Serb Republic of BH Presidency. Regarding the treatment of war prisoners, do you recall what measures, if any, were taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what measures were taken. I know that the Defence Minister drafted the text of that order and I believe that through the General Staff, he forwarded it to various commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I seek a clarification. What do you mean by "the text of that order"? Are you referring to the order mentioned under agenda item 14, the "order of the Serb Republic of BH Presidency regarding the treatment of war prisoners"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I knew that the Defence Minister was preparing such an order and that I'm sure that through the General Staff, the order was forwarded to various commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That must have been prior to this discussion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it -- did it happen at other occasions as well that a minister would draft an order which would then be issued by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the customary procedure ought to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit P64, P65 in the Treanor presentation, and I think also introduced as P443 - we should check that to see if there is a duplication - is an order of June 13th that appears in the -- appeared in the Official Gazette on that date. Perhaps, and it may offer some clarification, I have one copy of it. If it could be placed on the ELMO, perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not that much confused but you asked what measures were taken and the witness referred to something in the logic should have happened before the discussion so I was mainly seeking to clarify the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just going to start one step at a time by identifying the order, if it can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can put it on the ELMO if we put it on the ELMO and if the B/C/S original would be in the hands of the witness. Mr. Usher, I see that the B/C/S original -- there's another copy available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, the exhibit before you is the instructions on the treatment of captured persons, the headings indicates on the basis of the order of the Presidency, the Minister of Defence issued instructions and I believe we see on the second page, which is not currently on the ELMO, the name and signature of Colonel Bogdan Subotic. First of all, is that the order that you were just referring to in the -- discussing the agenda item?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It most likely is; however, I cannot be fully certain that this is the exact text that we reviewed. I know that on several occasions, Colonel Subotic drafted instructions or orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after receipt of information that occurrences of unlawful treatment of war prisoners had taken place, what measures, if any, were taken to ensure the application of either this order or any other order that directed itself to the treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in addition to the measures we have seen in these documents, there were no other steps taken by the government. I also know that in addition to this instruction, Colonel Subotic also drafted some orders on behalf of the president and the Supreme Command. The minutes do mention an order and not instructions; therefore, it is quite possible that at that time, what we had in front of us was one of these orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think the minutes say an order of -- by the Serb Republic of BH Presidency and looking at the exhibit in front of you, which was P65 Treanor tab 12, or at binder 12, tab 159, it states, "On the basis of the order of the president." I don't know if that clarifies it for you in any way but I direct your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not deny that it says here that the instructions are being issued on the basis of the order; however, I know that I saw in his hands also the orders that he was drafting. So I can't be sure whether it's the instructions that we discussed at that time or some of the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the scale or nature of occurrences of unlawful treatment that were made known to members of the government or any other political authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger, I'd like to ask a question. Witness, I would like to ask you the following question: When in government session, it is stated that war prisoners have not been treated according to the law, and that the order issued by the president of the Serb Republic has not been complied with, who was in charge of reporting to the president or to the Presidency? In other words, was it the case that the Presidency was systematically informed of anything that was going wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that the General Staff had to have this information and the Defence Minister must have received his information from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what I would like to understand is how the institutions worked. For example, if we have a look at these minutes that were established after each session, were they systematically sent to the Presidency, these minutes? Was someone in charge of reporting to the Presidency? Was this organised, institutionalised? You must be aware of that because I repeat it once again, you were the Deputy Prime Minister. How did all this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the minutes were regularly sent to them. There was no regular practice of sending them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But following each session, was someone in charge of reporting to the Presidency? What had been going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prime Minister attended Presidency sessions. I don't think that that took place on a daily basis but at least several times a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I would have one additional question to that as well. Did you ever experience, in your communications, conversations with members of the Presidency, that they were unaware of any issue you wanted to raise, you wanted to discuss, or you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you indicated that you believed that information regarding unlawful treatment of prisoners would be made known to the Defence Minister, that was Mr. Subotic and he was present at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document we looked at before, that is the instructions on the treatment of captured persons, indicates in its last paragraph, paragraph 19, that, "The commission for the exchange of prisoners operating under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall also function as an information bureau for providing information on captured persons." And that head of the Ministry of Justice was Momcilo Mandic and he was also present at that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated early your in your testimony as reflected in remarks at the 19th or the 22nd Assembly session held in Zvornik in November, and remarks by you and by Mr. Djeric that Mr. Stanisic, in addition to Mr. Mandic, were reporting to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Stanisic was also present at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, I believe you indicated earlier in your testimony in discussing the ICRC agreement number 2 in Geneva in May of 1992, which was signed by Mr. Kalinic, that he often reported to Mr. Karadzic. Is that right and was he also present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you indicated on Tuesday, when discussing the information available to you and others, and during the course of a discussion about the extent of the territories that were controlled by Bosnian Serb forces and where those territories were and whether they also encompassed areas where the Muslims were or had been a majority, that every Assembly session was opened with a report on the political situation and the situation in the theatres of war -- excuse me, that's just for the benefit of counsel and the Court, that's in the area of 11-5-29 and 11-5-30. And you also indicated that you were given the information and could take notice of it but you stated that you were not able to respond in terms of saying that someone made a wrong decision or had advocated a position with which you didn't agree. Do you generally recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn, then, to tab 79 which contain the transcript of an Assembly session held on the 26th of July, 1992. Tab 79 is in binder 2. Mr. Trbojevic, tab 79 reflects the taperecording of the 17th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on 25 and 26 July, as you can see from the beginning. It was chaired by Mr. Krajisnik who opens the session with some remarks. Your remarks at that session, although I don't -- well, first of all, may I ask you, I don't need to direct your attention to your remarks at that session if you recall attending that session at the -- in the latter part of July 1992. Your remarks are reflected at page 43 of the English translation, and in your copy, that would be page 41, I believe -- no, excuse me, page 42, toward the bottom. I'm actually going to direct your attention to remarks of others at that session, Mr. Trbojevic. First of all, recalling our -- the testimony the other day about the extent of territory that had been -- that the Bosnian Serb forces were in control of, we discussed figures ranging from 65 to 70 per cent. Perhaps I can ask you to turn this would be page 38 of the English translation and page -- beginning at page 37 and extending into page 38 of the B/C/S translation before you, Mr. Trbojevic. Those are the remarks by Mrs. Plavsic. If you could look at her comments beginning at about the fourth sentence of the second paragraph of her remarks, she states that, "65 per cent of Serb territory belong to our people according to the cadastre and 70 per cent of the conquered one which is only 5 per cent gain in relation to the previous number." So was that one occasion on which you were informed of the extent of territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina that had been acquired by Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was evidently discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that's a reflection of the same thing you were telling us yesterday, that some of the information you received, you received at Assembly sessions during the course of discussions about the military and political situation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall also hearing at that session about problems with captured Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether we discussed this, but if you could refer me to the page in order to remind myself of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. If I could ask you to turn to page 31 of the B/C/S copy, that'd be page 32 of the English translation. Those are comments by Mr. Milanovic. His remarks begin at page 28 of the English. The portion to which I'm directing your attention, Mr. Trbojevic, as I say is found at your page 31, and the English translation, page 32. And Mr. Milanovic states, "We have a huge problem with captured people of other nationalities. We have hundreds and thousands of these prisoners." It appears to be in the course of a discussion by Mr. Milanovic identifying various problems to which he wants to bring the attention of the people gathered at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, your microphone was on -- it's now off again. We heard your typing but it's now off again. Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that Dr. Milanovic talked about there being a large number of captured persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the nature of the huge problem with these captured people was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what Dr. Milanovic had in mind while talking about it here. He was the vice-president of the Assembly, otherwise a physician from Banja Luka. He must have possessed some information. I can't really glean from the text here what else he might have had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this information, as related by Dr. Milanovic, trigger any action by you or any other of the political officials assembled at the Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond that which we have already discussed here, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also receive information at that session regarding the forcible displacement or expulsion of Muslims or other non-Serbs from areas now controlled by the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Not any information about forcible displacement. I don't think anybody mentioned anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to page 67 of the B/C/S version in front of you and page 66 of the English. Those pages reflect the remarks of Mr. Prstojevic who says at the beginning of his remarks, "Mr. President, honourable MPs, I have decided to say a few words and to ask a few questions that I am being asked by the citizens of Sarajevo. Namely, when the Serbs started the uprise rising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain areas, there was no government or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive in the first couple of days. When we learned that he was alive, and when he visited us in Ilidza, and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." First of all, did you know at that time, who Mr. Prstojevic was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was the president of the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did his -- did the information he provided the -- those gathered at the Assembly, including yourself, that the -- he and the Serbs from his area had extended their territory by driving the Muslims out the areas where they had been a majority trigger any particular reaction that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may comment on this. I think that they viewed this as a result, as a consequence of war operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may comment further upon the municipality of Ilidza, it is located on the opposite side of Sarajevo in relation to Pale. The issue of access to Ilidza was a problematical one because there was no access to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it, in fact. Next to it was the town of Hadzici which was under Muslim control as well as the surrounding areas so that what was at issue here was the very survival of this municipality. Therefore, this piece of information that Muslims had been driven away from a part of this municipality was not regarded as any sort of a conquest of the area, but simply trying to secure access to the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the difference between conquest and simply securing access to the area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree with you, yes, that there is no difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in your familiarity with what you called war operations in that area. Are you familiar, for example, what happened in Gornji Kotorac in roughly May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was going on. I can't even say whether in relation to what Prstojevic was remarking here, whether there was some sort of a military action involved there but the government did not react to this in any way. I don't know what was going on in Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can turn to some information on events in the Birac area. That would be found at -- well let's begin at about page 74 of the B/C/S and page 72 of the English translation. You can see on page 71 of the translation that it's Mr. Dukic speaking, Rajko Dukic. Mr. Dukic had been, for quite a time, the president of the SDS Executive Board; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look at a portion of Mr. Dukic's remarks found toward the bottom of page 72 after what appeared to be some complaints about the extent of success of the Serbian forces, Mr. Dukic states, "So I'm asking you, gentlemen, why we expelled all Muslim judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik? Will we be accused then, I hope we will not, but will these others be better there working like this? I would be ashamed and I would regret all the victims if I lived in a state in which Muslims and Muslim ideology would judge -- and where their justice was done." Further down in Mr. Dukic's remarks, approximately the middle of the page 73 in English and in yours, page 75, sir, Mr. Dukic notes, "If question move further, there is Birac which is 100 to 108 kilometres away and has 120.000 Muslims. That is -- that is how many there were but I hope that has at least been halved and 90.000 Serbs." Do you recall, Mr. Trbojevic, whether the remarks of Mr. Dukic at the 17th session triggered any action by any member of the government or any other member of the political authorities who were at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody acted upon this. I know that Dukic approached Djeric and talked to him on several occasions. I know that he also spoke to Karadzic before and after because that's what his status was. As for any official reaction after this meeting, I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the area that Mr. Dukic is referring to, Birac, is the same area that was the -- where Major Andric was a commander at the time he issued the order regarding the moving out of the Muslim population and the placement of men fit for military service into camps for exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Birac is an area extending down the slope of the mountain into the valley in the direction of Vlasenica and Zvornik. That's the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recall reviewing the order of Major Andric the other day and he was indicated as the Birac Commander or excuse me, the Commander of the Birac Brigade, that's the same area where Mr. Dukic is talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this information, Mr. Trbojevic, wasn't there also information made available at this session regarding what was happening in the Muslim population even beyond expulsions and even beyond their placement into camps, that is, indications that Muslims were being killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond war operations, I don't know whether there were any other types of information provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall anybody saying that the Bosnian Serbs had been chosen by the -- by Europe or by the International Community to be the Muslims' executioners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that something that you think you would have reacted to if you'd heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have reacted there and then at the session, but definitely if such a statement had been made, it amounted, then, to nonsense, utmost nonsense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 40 of the English, and page 40 of the B/C/S, please. That portion of the transcript reflects remarks by Mr. Nedic. And he states, "I am against solving the situation in Bosnia in haste. We must admit that the Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be. I do not want the Serb people to be executioners but I am also against us giving up our state, our land, and our territory." Did Mr. Nedic's remarks reflect any kind of general consensus at that Assembly session that acquiring the land, territory and state was going to involve the Serbs being the executioners of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedic was not able to properly express his own views let alone those of others. He was a peculiar sort of man who there, from the rostrum, invited, called upon Izetbegovic to return to prison because he had previously been serving a sentence there. His remarks for the most part boiled down to irresponsible scenes. You can see here that he is invoking some sort of a plan dating 800 or 1.000 years back in history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you find irresponsible, what was the nature of the irresponsibility of his remarks, Mr. Nedic's remarks, in what way do you find them irresponsible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. The interpreters didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, would you please repeat your answer, the interpreters could not hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked me what was irresponsible about this text which is quoted under the name of Nedic and I said that everything in here is irresponsible including his claim that some 700 to 800 years prior to that, there was a centre which had planned the events that we were taking part in then and that we ought to be executioners executing some other nation and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, may I ask you for a clarification. In your previous question to the witness, you asked him whether he recalled anybody saying that the Bosnian Serbs had been chosen by Europe or by the International Community to be the Muslims' executioners and then when the witness said "I don't remember," then you took him to page 40 and 41. In the remarks of Mr. Nedic, I do not see any reference to the International Community or Europe. Is that a mistake on my part or is that -- could you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Your Honour, and the question was not framed precisely but I think it did direct your attention to the appropriate portion of the text that I wanted to discuss. But I'm not suggesting via that question that there's another portion of Mr. Nedic's remarks that indicate who planted the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the view of how the examination goes, perhaps some special caution would be proper, Mr. Tieger, in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However, I will -- I think Mr. Trbojevic mentioned a portion of Mr. Nedic's remarks about an 800-year-old plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Trbojevic, you were mentioning the remarks by Mr. Nedic at the beginning of his comments where he said "This which is happening" - I take that to mean a reference to this portion - "this which is happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina today was planned 700 to 800 years ago in one of the world's power centres and this which is happening today is by no means new."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said, this is what is stated in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. But were when you were indicated what you found irresponsible about the remarks, I understood you to be pointing out in part those portions of his remarks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, including that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you find to be irresponsible about his remarks that the Serbs are to be the Muslims' executioners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the entire statement was irresponsible and that it represented an outburst, that it did not, in fact, represent anyone's position or anyone's view. He claims here that the Muslims have been planted on us as a nation, which is ludicrous. He claims that someone else had envisaged Serbs as executioners of the other nation which, once again, is completely unfounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that he said that could be acceptable is this bit here where he says that he doesn't want the Serbs to be executioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that reflect what was actually happening on the ground, that is, that Muslims were being killed at such a scale that it could be said, as a general matter, that they are being executed as a people, it seems, in this comment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge regarding that, and I don't think that it could be said in that way. The exception to that would naturally be the events in Srebrenica that have become known now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would have been the appropriate reaction if that view of the conflict and of the consequences of the conflict had been confirmed by a member of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the questions are now entering into a realm of hypothesis and speculation which is really outside the scope of proper examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's eliminate any hypothesis and speculation, Your Honour, and perhaps we can turn to another portion of the transcript. Before we do, I have one more question about this page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is, we see that Vojin Kupresanin, can you please tell us quickly who Mr. Kupresanin was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin is from Banja Luka, an MP, and I don't know whether, at the time, he was the president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn, please, to page 88 of the B/C/S, that's page 86 of the English translation. That page reflects remarks by Mr. Karadzic at that session, his remarks begin at page 85 in the English, page 87 of the B/C/S. In approximately the middle of page 86 of the English and I believe somewhere toward the top of page 88 in the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic states the following: "There is truth in what Mr. Kupresanin has said, although nobody in Europe will say it openly, that this conflict was roused in order to eliminate the Muslims." Did Dr. Karadzic's remarks reflect his understanding of events on the ground as far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They most likely did. He certainly didn't say this off the cuff, he must have prepared before he took the floor and it contains certain elements that he mentioned several times, on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what other occasions did you hear Dr. Karadzic make remarks that contained these elements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke several times in various assemblies, in Sarajevo before he left the town, and also in our assemblies in the clubs of deputies. He would say that we -- that the Muslims want to create their own state but that we do not want them to overwhelm us by numbers, to become dominant through numbers. This thesis that Europe wants to protect itself from the Muslim invasion and a result of that has provoked a war in the Balkans in order to prevent that, these are things that were mentioned more than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, and so he was saying -- and since the Muslims are being destroyed as a consequence of this war, then Europe must have intended that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a view. You know, sometimes, he would say it in a very vivid way. He would say, "We don't want to win by using just one arm." He would also say, "We don't mind them having their own state, they can have their own state, it's just that it should be without us." This is something that was mentioned several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the corollary was also true, and our state should also be without them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this thesis that a state must be pure was never verbalised. I don't think it was ever uttered and even if you scruitinise the documents in the most thorough way, you probably wouldn't find that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If not stated explicitly, was it understood in other ways?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was implied or understood in other ways because even though we had all kinds of constitutional amendments, this statement never crept into the Constitution, it never was allowed into the constitutional text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was expressed concern, wasn't there, about the number of Muslims who would be in Serb territories because of Muslim birth rates, Muslim demographics?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take the opportunity to ask for one question. You said the corollary, that is, "us but without them" was never stated. Mr. Tieger then asked you if it was understood, and your answer came down to approximately: It was not understood because it never got its place in the text of the Constitution even when amended. That is not a complete answer to that question since even if it does not appear in the constitution, a matter could still be understood. Therefore, let me directly ask you: Was it envisaged, once there would be a separate Serb entity or state, whatever you call it, and a separate Muslim state, was it envisaged that in that Serb state, there would remain a substantial number of non-Serbs living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who made what kind of analyses; however, I'm certain that it was not understood that the territory of Republika Srpska ought to exist without Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "Not without," what would be, let's say, acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not negotiate. We did not bargain on this issue, so I cannot answer your question. We never discussed whether 30 per cent was too much, or 20 per cent was too little. There were no such discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in those parts where there was a majority of Muslims, was that a situation that would be accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintain that I did not hear anyone at the level of leadership saying that the numbers ought to be reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then put it in a different way. Is there any part of the territory of Republika Srpska which had a majority non-Serb population before the armed conflict that still had a majority non-Serb population after the hostilities had ended, the armed hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know statistical figures. As far as I know, the territory of the city of Bijeljina had a majority of Muslim population and exactly what the numbers were in each municipality, I think the answer is no; however, I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, we've seen references in the Assembly to expulsions of Muslims, the confinement of Muslims and Croats, to Serbs becoming the executioners of Muslims, to the concern about Muslim birth rates. You said that you never heard anyone in the leadership say that the numbers had to be reduced. Was it understood, as a result of sessions like this and other contacts among political figures that the numbers were being reduced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not make such a conclusion and I don't think that the others had any reason to draw such a conclusion. Now, as to whether there were some people who had already crystalised such views, perhaps. I can't claim that there weren't such people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated the other day that you would hear things at Assembly sessions and learn information at Assembly sessions but that you made a point of saying you couldn't always -- you couldn't do anything about some of the things that you heard, you couldn't tell a General he was wrong, you couldn't essentially challenge a position. So first let me ask you, are these views that you agreed with or didn't agree with, the ones we've looked at in this Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, you're putting a general question to me. There are many elements with which I disagreed, but I can't say that I disagreed with everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these remarks or positions or the inferences to be drawn from them or the inferences that were drawn from them by you cause you, as Deputy Minister, to take any action whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand from what happened at that session that the events that were being discussed, including the reduction of Muslims as reflected in the remarks of Mr. Dukic, the confinement of Muslims and Croats as reflected in the remarks by Mr. Nedic, and the other elements we've discussed, would stop or would continue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My expectations were such that I wanted the state of war to be brought to an end as soon as possible, to have the peace process commenced and to ensure that the peace reigned in that area as soon as possible. Most sincerely, we hoped, with each new negotiating -- peace negotiation, that a way would be found to put an end to hostilities. Nobody in their right mind could either go along with a wish upon the people to be confined, to be killed in their confinement, and to be afforded a treatment which is contrary to human dignity. The settlement was not possible without cessation of war operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic talked about the amount of conquered territory, Mr. Nedic remarked that he didn't want the Serbs to be executioners but he wanted the state, the land, and the territory. Were there any indications by members of the Bosnian Serb leadership that there would be continued efforts to acquire Serbian ethnic territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that such a statement could be put forward because even the Cutileiro Plan had envisaged certain frameworks for ethnic communities and the Serb side accepted that plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the events we've just been -- and the consequences we've just been looking at were the result, weren't they, of efforts to gain control of what were regarded as Serbian ethnic territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, when a war erupts in a certain territory, a war between three sides, where each side is fighting the other two, then very little can be planned. Each side in the military sense tried to put as much territory as possible under its control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't the Bosnian Serb leadership insist on the acquisition of what were regarded as Bosnian Serb territories?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not insist. In a number of such meetings and sessions, not only Assembly ones, there were objections voiced both by members of the General Staff and other officers about the fact that a political position had not been clearly defined and that there were no conclusions reached or a position taken as to what areas ought to be conquered and then defended; rather, the troops were sent to the front line without an actual goal, without knowing why is it that we were waging a war in that area and not in another area and so on. And if you're interested, I can illustrate this with one of the Assembly sessions where some of us MPs objected and said, "Why is it that the team representing us in international negotiations does not address the MPs with a proposal of our final clearly defined political position?" Then, Karadzic gave the following answer: We objected to the fact that numerous proposals of the International Community and various other figures were not being accepted while simultaneously, we were failing do clearly define our political position and say what it is that we wanted. Karadzic explained this with the following sentence, "We will not accept any plan. We will accept what we are forced to accept," which, in my sincere view, was ridiculous. But that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And didn't Mr. Krajisnik say at this very session we've been looking at that there were territories that were not yet under the control of the Bosnian Serbs but which should be part of the Bosnian Serb republic because they're ethnic territories? Let me direct your attention to page 49 of the B/C/S and page 49 of the English. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Do you see that about a dozen lines down, Mr. Trbojevic? "Also there are territories which are not under our control now but which should be part of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina due to them being ethnic territories."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your remarks just a moment ago that there were no goals. Doesn't Mr. Krajisnik refer to those ethnic territories in the course of talking about the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that Republika Srpska should include the ethnic territories held by the Serbian people. That is where the Serb people lived. And this, here, they refer actually to the territories where the Serb people used to live prior to World War II when genocide was committed against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where Muslims now constituted a majority; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of your forecast yesterday that you'd finish your examination-in-chief by the first break ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would ask for this indulgence of the Court. If in the break, I have an opportunity to -- I am very close, I can assure you of that, and it's close enough so I wouldn't ask at this point directly for more time but I would ask an opportunity to look over my documents and see if there's anything left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are then allowed not to express yourself on whether this finishes your examination-in-chief, but to express yourself after the break and then depending on what you are asking we'll see to what extent we can meet your request. We adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask for permission for another basically I won't say one question but one series of questions arising from directly from what we were just discussing and I can assure the Court we will -- that I will, nevertheless, finish within the earlier estimate. I suspect I'm talking about five to ten minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, that would approximately compensate the time taken by the Chamber before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's very kind, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, during the discussion before the break, I asked you at one point -- you mentioned at one point "their state without us" and I asked if the corollary was true, "our state without them," and you stated that this thesis that a state must be pure was never verbalised. I'd like you, please, to look at Exhibit 292 KID 3081. That's a video and transcript, Your Honour -- it's a recording, excuse me. And for the benefit of the interpreters, the portion of the recording that will be played can be found at the begin -- beginning at the bottom of ERN page 0361-7691, I think beginning the second line from the bottom. In the English, found at page 4, approximately eight lines down. It's a recording from the deputies' club of 28 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Look at these priests of ours, every time we discuss with great respect and then we say, "God help the Serbian people to agree." No one has the right to do that by bypassing or unity. I tell you, everything we do in this parliament, everything I do personally, I do exclusively for pure areas of -- and Herzegovina and -- and I will not yield the right to tell the people of Krajina that they are not right. The people of Krajina are not working for the whole Serbian people, but we are working for the people of Krajina. But that is difficult to prove." Mr. Trbojevic, you're gesturing. Did you have -- were you able to hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just a brief clip, but at a certain point we couldn't hear the recording anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a brief clip, Mr. Trbojevic, that's what it intended. The only thing we have to find out was whether the clip you heard was any shorter. Where did it finish? The last part I heard was the line, "But that is difficult to prove." Did you hear that portion? Could you have a look at the page with the last four digits is -- I think it was 7691, Mr. Tieger, upper part. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you just perhaps read the part and see where you -- where it stopped for you. Could you tell us what was the last line you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That wasn't intelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You couldn't understand any part of it. Could we replay it, Mr. Tieger, and could we perhaps make clear to the witness where your clip starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It starts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 7691, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, where the words "ivo nasi."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found that, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The two last lines of 0361-7691 and then we replay it and please -- Mr. Usher, could you also show to the witness where the volume button is so that he can -- let's then replay that portion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Look at these priests of ours: Every time we discuss with great respect and then we say, "God help the Serbian people to agree," no one has the right to do that by bypassing our unity. I tell you everything we do in this parliament, everything I do personally, I do exclusively for pure areas of -- and Herzegovina, and -- and I will not yield the right to tell the people of Krajina that they are not right. The people of Krajina are not working for the whole Serbian people, but we are working for the people of Krajina. But that is difficult to prove."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you hear it, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the voice of the speaker, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is Krajisnik's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you heard this recording here today, had you heard Mr. Krajisnik, on any previous occasion, speak about pure areas and the -- or that everything he did, he did exclusively for pure areas?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at a session of the deputies' club on February 28th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the Assembly session at which the temperature and the tensions heightened, so to speak, between Radovan Karadzic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the other name.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the date itself of the 28th of February doesn't really tell me much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the second name, you said the tension between Radovan Karadzic and the second name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radoslav Brdjanin. This bit does look like it's from that session because Mr. Krajisnik is addressing people from Krajina as if he was talking about the clearing up of the relations that have something to do with them -- or the clearing up of the positions [Interpreter's note].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Trbojevic, let me ask you this question. We looked at the remarks made in July and the events that were reflected in those remarks. What was happening on the ground at that time and is reflected in the remarks that -- that we looked at before the break were moving Republika Srpska toward a state that was more ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expression "ethnically pure" was not uttered by either myself or any of the persons involved in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The things they described, the expulsions, the reduction of Muslims, the Serbs being Muslims' executioners were moving Republika Srpska towards a more ethnically-pure state, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have mentioned several elements in your question and I cannot agree to the question as it is put, cannot give an affirmative answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reduction of Muslims on the territories controlled by Bosnian Serbs in the ways we saw reflected in the comments at that session, was that moving Republika Srpska toward a more ethnically-pure state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, to the extent I heard about the policies as discussed at Assembly sessions, there was no such policy with a view to reducing the numbers of Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and creating "pure" territories. Now, whether a sentence or two taken from here might serve as an introduction to the affirmations that you are putting forth here, perhaps, I might agree to that extent. But such a policy did not exist as a position or as an orientation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sense, if any, did it exist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you already several times that it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've told me several times, there wasn't an explicit policy then you said, "The thesis that a state must be pure was never verbalised." Now, we just looked at Mr. Krajisnik saying that everything he did was for pure territories. To what extent did that reflect an orientation towards the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think that what was meant here was ethnically-pure territories. I don't know what the background or the context in which these words were uttered was. The section we heard was inadequate and inadequately clear in order for me to be able to say that this was, in fact, the position in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before Mr. Stewart, I'll give the Defence the opportunity to cross-examine the witness, I'd like to raise one practical issue. The witness, not necessarily be present or absent, I don't think it makes much difference. Mr. Trbojevic, if you would allow us for just a few minutes. One of the issues we should deal with is a schedule he had for the undecided 92 bis applications. The Chamber is a bit concerned about the 92 bis applications, they are pending for a very, very long time, at least as far as I remember, the sixth motion dates back from 2002 when you were not even involved, Mr. Stewart. The seventh from somewhere mid-2003, and the eighth from, I think it was January 2004. Perhaps I could hand out just a schedule of -- yes, if that could be given to the parties, one for the Defence, one's for the Prosecution. As usual, the 92 bis witnesses are split up to some extent, in batches, so that we can deal with it. But of course we couldn't deal with 92 bis applications in a more -- or stretched them and delay them for such a long time then finally the Prosecution's case would be finished and then we are still dealing with 92 bis applications. Therefore, this is the next batch the Chamber would like to present to you to -- there will be another batch which will be a batch of experts but this is the one at hand at this moment where pages are mentioned. These are not the highlighted pages but are pages of the material as presented. For example, if I draw your attention to the 1006, that's the semi-ultimate transcript, that's the second from the bottom, you would see that it's approximately not more than 50 per cent which is highlighted, so these numbers cover the pages in total and not necessarily the relevant pages. Similar, for example, is the cover pages for statements. The Chamber would suggest that by Friday, the 22nd of April, that's a little bit more than two weeks from now when the Defence would make submissions and then the OTP would respond not later than the 29th of April. I just put it in front of you. Is there any comments on that? Mr. Tieger, any problem with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of any at the moment. I actually had some discussions with Mr. Gaynor about that earlier today, but I should probably caution that I'd be much more comfortable making a representation about this after consultation with Mr. Gaynor who's been working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart. You would also need the next break or -- because I'm aware that Ms. Loukas is also heavily involved in 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, sorry, did Your Honour say the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, to comment on the time schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest respect, a person needs a little bit more than the next break to deal with this sort of thing. It's -- of course, the Prosecution don't have any particular problem that immediately springs to mind because all they'll have to do is respond to our response to their application which has been put together in the first place. But Mr. Tieger, quite reasonably, asks for the opportunity of consulting his team. But the idea that I can consult Ms. Loukas in the next break over all this material and discuss with her what's involved with these witnesses is simply ridiculous, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it could not come as a surprise, could it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does not come as a surprise, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: More than one week ago, you were informed about that the next batch had to be established and what would be in that batch and now to say, "Well this is all new," is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't say that, Your Honour, with respect, I didn't say that at all. I sent an e-mail to the Trial Chamber -- I was presented in about three lines with a suggested time table. I wrote back and said in very clear but I hope entirely courteous terms that the time table suggested was simply completely unrealistic. And it is, Your Honour. And I would ask, by the way, for the witness to leave. I do not -- I suggest it's not appropriate for the witness to sit here. He understands English very well and it's embarrassing for him and it's not appropriate. We do have some issues to resolve, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't foresee that this would be your reaction. Perhaps we spend some time at the beginning of the next session and pay proper attention to it and that you will be allowed -- unless you say I can deal with it in five minutes, then we'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom and -- but I do not want the -- a discussion to take the next half an hour or three quarters of an hour and in the meantime, losing time for examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I will undertake to do, of course, I will, of course, speak, if I can get a hold of her, which expect to do. I will of course speak to Ms. Loukas in the next break, because that will at least enable to me to report as constructively as I can, which is aim, at the beginning of the next session, as Your Honour helpfully offers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's do that and then Mr. Stewart, are you ready to start cross-examination of Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did wonder whether I -- a lectern could be brought across the court with a warning to the usher not to break his leg on my power lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll give you the fresh lectern. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it's correct, isn't it, that you had no personal contact with Mr. Krajisnik before May 1992 except in the rather unusual sense that you had been a judge in a case in which Mr. Krajisnik was one of the defendants.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you arrived, you told Their Honours, in Pale, shortly after the Republika Srpska Assembly which had been held, although not in Pale, on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived, I believe, on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was, at that time, a matter of some urgency and importance for Republika Srpska to constitute a fully-functioning government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. With your permission, just a minute ago, I said I had not seen Mr. Krajisnik before 1992 - I said that in response to your question - which is not entirely true. We started meeting in the course of 1990 just prior to the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just pause and get the questions straight, Mr. Trbojevic, so we can go as clearly as possible through it. I had asked you whether you had had any -- well I put it to you, you'd had no personal contact with Mr. Krajisnik and then a moment ago, you were qualifying the answer by saying that you'd said you'd not seen Mr. Krajisnik, not exactly literally what you'd said, but your -- so I would like to ask you, then, if you're going on to describe some sort of meeting or contact with Mr. Krajisnik in the course of 1990, to indicate to the Trial Chamber very clearly the nature of that contact. What was your first contact with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what was the first contact; however, the elections were being prepared and Mr. Koljevic called me to ask for my permission to be placed on the ticket of the SDS in that election. Then, under those circumstances, we met several times, not just the two of us but a group of people including Mr. Koljevic, Karadzic, Dukic, Professor Lejovac, somewhat later, Mrs. Plavsic as well, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the period before you arrived in Pale in May 1992, is it nevertheless correct that you had never had any meeting with Mr. Krajisnik at which just you and he had been present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elections were held in late 1990. Mr. Krajisnik became president of the Assembly. I was an MP. We did see each other at the sessions of the deputies' club, Assembly sessions. Several times, the two of us met in his office when he was the president of the Assembly discussing some current issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are talking -- in that last answer, are you talking about occasions in his office when it was just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office, yes, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these relatively routine meetings that a deputy might have with the speaker or president of the Assembly of which he was a member?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any significant importance or weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those meetings in Mr. Krajisnik's office the only occasions that you say that you and he met just the two of you for, and I'm leaving aside, I'm leaving for the moment before you went to Pale and before 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those other meetings that you referred to when you described a group of people including Mr. Koljevic, Karadzic, Dukic, Professor Lejovac, later Mrs. Plavsic, was this an informal group or was this some group that had a title or a designated structure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain situations, it was an informal group. In some situations, we met as the deputies' club of the Serbian Democratic Party. And in some situations, it was a meeting which was called "party's council" or something like that, perhaps "council for relations with other political parties," but it did have a title. And Dr. Lejovac chaired that council. In those meetings, there would be 30 or more people. I occasionally attended those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the meetings that you have mentioned then at which those particular people were present, as you described, Dr. Karadzic, Professor Lejovac and so on, those were meetings of a larger number of people but including some or, on occasions, all of those people; is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The council existed before the elections. I think that afterwards, there were no meetings of that council, at least I did not attend any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no -- there was no small group which included Mr. Koljevic, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Dukic, and you, was there, no group of six or ten people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not exist as a group that met several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that -- that group of people that you've said including, and you said, Koljevic, Karadzic, Dukic, Lejovac, later Mrs. Plavsic, at that time, Mr. Krajisnik, was he a member of that group, as you have described it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't -- up to the time when you came to Pale in May 1992, you didn't, in any serious sense, know Mr. Krajisnik personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known him from the time when we had court proceedings, when we were preparing for elections. I also know him from the period after the Assembly was constituted, when we had some activities on the eve of the war operations, when we were discussing such issues as will Bosnia and Herzegovina seek independence or not. So occasionally, we would meet in smaller or larger groups to discuss these issues and both Mr. Krajisnik and I would be present. So these were our contacts when both of us attended the same sessions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, Mr. Trbojevic, you were not -- you were not -- you and Mr. Krajisnik were not personal friends, you were not close acquaintances, you didn't have any particular knowledge or involvement in each other's personal or family lives in any way, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So coming, then, back to May 1992, when you arrived in Pale, you agreed that it was an urgent matter to constitute a fully-functioning government for Republika Srpska, and the position at that time of conflict was that there was not a huge pool of well-qualified candidates to form such a government, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Trbojevic, this doesn't imply any disparagement or attack on your own qualifications, but your arrival in Pale as somebody with some political experience and your legal experience and qualifications, meant that you were a -- a very useful person for Republika Srpska to have arrive in Pale, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's correct, isn't it, that Dr. Karadzic, for example, was keen to use whatever powers he had to appoint you to get you into the government without waiting for the next Assembly to go through the formalities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge regarding that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know any details yourself, do you, about consultation of Dr. Karadzic by Mr. Djeric in relation to your proposed appointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The evidence was -- the evidence that Mr. Stewart is clearly referring to was regarding Mr. Djeric's consultation with Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just -- do you intend to say that Mr. Stewart is not reflecting the testimony given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also could say it in a different way, that Mr. Stewart is challenging the evidence given by the witness. Would that be what you are doing, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I were to put to the witness that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the matter is clear and Mr. Stewart challenges, perhaps, some of the evidence of the witness. I expect him to do that on a more regular basis. He does not confront the witness with his testimony, he's just putting similar matters in a different way. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, it is correct, isn't it, that you don't know details of the consultation of Dr. Karadzic by Mr. Djeric in relation to your proposed appointment, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, perhaps you first refer us to the lines you have in mind because you certainly will have them somewhere in your mind. I think it's Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you have a page number for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I only have the -- I don't have the LiveNote from Monday, unfortunately, so let me correlate that quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is I don't have the LiveNote because we were in a different courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can find it. Your Honour, it can be found at -- it starts at page -- I'm sorry, I found it quickly in both versions without referring to the pages, I can find it in a LiveNote -- in the regular version if somebody had it, but I don't. But I can tell the Court therefore several references to such consultations and not one of them failed to reflect reference to both people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Mr. Tieger's going to tell me I've got it wrong, he'd better tell me where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give two or three literal words in the right sequence, Madam Registrar could help us out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "For their consent" is such a word, we found it here. That's 11.406 and the preceding pages, I believe. I'm sorry, 11.406 and the subsequent pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, where am I to find this? I -- this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have LiveNote, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought the problem was we were in a different court or.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have it on your computer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought there was an insuperable problem. If there isn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- I have a problem in -- if you search for the line "Krajisnik gave their consent."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you are about at the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I need to get to the day, first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Monday, I said that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but how do I do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Monday, April 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Monday is not on your -- it was usually not on mine. That's the reason why I took the paper version, because I knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got the paper version. But I've got the paper version numbered one to whatever it was on Monday. If somebody gives me that page reference then I'm there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to be practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do not yet have the continuous transcript, Your Honour, as I think Your Honour understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is approximately the 30th page because the numbered transcript starts at 377 and it's on page 40 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do have a solution, I can get to it on my own laptop but it does take a second or so. I just found it on my laptop at the precise moment I've been handed the hard copy: Sorry, may I ask through Your Honour to Mr. Tieger where I am looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you're on the LiveNote with pages in approximately 11.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've been handed 11.406, 11.407 and 11.408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it starts on 11.407.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first reference I see on those pages on the transcript on the screen is at 11.406 at line 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was confronted with part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't for the life of me see in any way in which I have misstated or misrepresented any evidence or question to the witness in the course of my cross-examination. For the moment, I'm simply not understanding the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the concern at least as far as this testimony as detailed are concerned, is that the witness told us that he heard from Mr. Djeric that he got the consent. Whether you would consider that would be sufficient detail, perhaps on the basis of that, Mr. Stewart, you could -- whether Mr. Djeric told him when and how, I mean further details are possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm focussing, Your Honour, on the following: If I related that you and Judge Hanoteau had told me something and I said that several times about the -- my understanding of this communication that someone had with somebody else, and then questions arose about what Judge Orie -- or what you had heard Judge Orie said to that person, I think that's a misleading characterisation of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
